items.title: Earl Turbinton Interview, 1990-09-01
items.q: So it's like being a direct descendant of Sidney Bechet or Louis Cottrell or Willie Humphrey

ctx.x: I want the workshop remembered as a place for people to become cognizant of just the kind of sacrifice and dedication that musicians and all artists put into their work, uh, so that they can bring a part of themselves and a part of their experience in sharing themselves with people. Uh, to be remembered as a place that some of new, the seeds and the foundation of some of the greatest New Orleans music that you hear now and that you've heard in the past few years that what we at the workshop and all of those…

to explore some of these things. But when you come from New Orleans, you're a branch off the original tree. This is where it started. So it's like being a direct descendant of Sidney Bechet or Louis Cottrell or Willie Humphrey and on and on and on the great people that came afterwards. I learned from Alvin Baptiste and Wes Anderson learned from Alvin Baptiste and I taught Wes. And we all somehow wind up teaching each other either something of music or a life of spirituality or just sharing our lives together.…
Okay. Was that Clyde Kerr Sr. who said that to you? Who was your teacher who said that you came?
